questions.q: Why is data broken into small packets before being sent across the internet, rather than sent as one continuous stream?
keyPoints: Sharing/efficiency: packets from many users interleave over the same links, so no single transfer monopolises the connection
Resilience: each packet carries its destination address and is routed independently, so it can take a different path around congestion or a failed link
Error recovery: if one packet is lost or corrupted, only that small packet is resent, not the whole file
Each packet has a sequence number so the receiver can reassemble them in order and detect any missing
questions.explanation: Packets can arrive out of order, which is exactly why they are numbered.

questions.q: How does DNS resolve a domain name into an IP address?
keyPoints: DNS translates a human-readable domain name into the server's numeric IP address (the 'phone book of the internet')
It checks caches first; if not found, a recursive resolver walks a hierarchy: root server, then the top-level-domain (e.g. .com) servers, then the authoritative server
The authoritative server returns the IP, which is cached under a time-to-live (TTL) so later lookups skip the walk
The browser then uses that IP to connect; DNS itself does not fetch the page

questions.q: How does HTTPS (via TLS) secure data travelling between a browser and a server?
keyPoints: The server presents a certificate (with its domain and public key) signed by a trusted Certificate Authority, which authenticates the server's identity
Asymmetric encryption (public/private key pair) is used once to securely agree a shared session key
Fast symmetric encryption (same key both ways) then protects all the bulk traffic
The result is that intercepted traffic is unreadable cipher text instead of plain text
questions.explanation: Asymmetric solves key exchange without prior contact; symmetric makes ongoing traffic fast.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
keyPoints: Authentication verifies WHO you are — proving identity, e.g. checking a username and password
Authorisation determines WHAT you are allowed to do — the permissions your role grants once identified
Order: identity first, then permission (e.g. logging in vs. being able to see the admin dashboard)

questions.q: Why is security considered the defining characteristic of e-commerce, rather than just a nice-to-have?
keyPoints: The asset being protected is money and personal identity (card numbers, addresses, purchase history)
A breach is existential, not merely embarrassing: direct financial loss, legal liability, and destroyed customer trust
This forces requirements an ordinary site lacks: encrypted transactions, secure storage of payment data, strong authentication, input validation, and regulatory compliance

questions.q: What actually distinguishes a Progressive Web App (PWA) from an ordinary responsive website?
keyPoints: Responsive is about APPEARANCE — layout adapting to screen size; an ordinary site can be responsive
A PWA is about CAPABILITY — it is installable to the device via a manifest and works offline via a service worker
It can also do app-like things such as push notifications, which a standard site cannot
Looking good on mobile alone does NOT make something a PWA

questions.q: How does a service worker give a PWA offline capability?
keyPoints: A service worker is a background script that acts as a programmable proxy, intercepting every network request the app makes
On first load it caches the 'app shell' — the core HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and icons
When the network is unavailable, it serves those cached resources instead of failing, so the app still opens
It is the same caching idea used for performance, repurposed for offline; it requires HTTPS because it can intercept all traffic

questions.q: Why is client-side (browser) validation not enough — why must the back-end re-validate user input?
keyPoints: Client-side code runs on the user's own device, so it is visible and can be disabled, altered, or bypassed entirely
An attacker can send a request straight to the server endpoint without ever loading the page or its JavaScript
So the server (which the developer controls) must re-validate and sanitise everything
Rule: client-side validation is for convenience/UX; server-side validation is for security

questions.q: What is the role of the W3C, and does it enforce web standards?
keyPoints: The W3C is the international body (founded by Tim Berners-Lee) that develops open standards like HTML and CSS
Its main value is interoperability — pages work consistently across browsers, devices, and over time
Crucially it RECOMMENDS standards; it does not enforce them — browser vendors and developers adopt them voluntarily

questions.q: How do the characteristics of big data force changes to a web application's architecture?
keyPoints: High volume and velocity mean a single monolithic server cannot cope, so the app is split into independent microservices that each scale separately (e.g. scale video delivery far more than login)
This also gives fault isolation — one failing service doesn't bring down the whole system
High global request volume is handled by a CDN caching content on edge servers near users to cut latency
The exam skill is mapping each big-data property (volume/velocity/variety) to the specific architectural decision it forces

Data mining ANALYSES large datasets to discover previously unknown patterns, trends, and relationships
Mining is discovery of hidden insight (e.g. which shows are watched together); storage/querying is retrieval

questions.q: When would you choose a NoSQL database over an SQL (relational) database, and why?
keyPoints: Choose SQL when data is highly structured with clear relationships and needs reliable, consistent transactions (ACID) — e.g. banking or e-commerce orders
Choose NoSQL when data is flexible/semi-structured and must scale to huge volume — e.g. a social-media activity feed where each item may have different fields
The justification is a property of the DATA (structure vs. flexibility/volume), not 'newer is better'
NoSQL means 'not only SQL' — a different tool, not a replacement; many systems use both

questions.q: How does a parameterised query prevent SQL injection?
keyPoints: SQL injection works because gluing user input into a query string mixes data and command — a quote in the input can close the string early and the rest is run as SQL
A parameterised query (prepared statement) uses a placeholder and passes the value to the database separately
The database then treats the value strictly as literal data, never as executable SQL, so it cannot alter the command
Rule: never build SQL by string concatenation with user input — always parameterise

questions.q: Compare using an ORM with writing raw SQL for a web app's data layer.
keyPoints: An ORM maps tables to classes and rows to objects, generating the SQL automatically
ORM benefits: faster development, readable object-oriented code, automatic relationships, and database portability
ORM costs: an abstraction layer with performance overhead, can generate inefficient queries, and doesn't remove the need to understand SQL
Raw SQL gives maximum control and performance but is more verbose and error-prone; a hybrid (ORM for routine CRUD, raw SQL for complex reports) is common

questions.q: What is the difference between a library and a framework?
keyPoints: A library is code that YOUR code calls when you want — you keep control of the application's structure
A framework provides the overall structure and calls YOUR code at defined points — this is inversion of control ('you call a library; a framework calls you')
Practical trade-off: a framework gives speed and consistency but locks you into its conventions; a library gives freedom but you build more of the structure yourself

questions.q: How does CSS improve the maintainability of a web application?
keyPoints: It enforces separation of concerns — HTML=structure, CSS=presentation, JavaScript=behaviour — kept in separate layers
Styling for a whole site lives in one external stylesheet, so a change (e.g. brand colour) is made once and applies everywhere
Design tokens (CSS custom properties) strengthen this further as single sources of truth
The opposite — inline styles scattered through the HTML — means editing hundreds of places for one change

questions.q: What does a web application's back-end actually do with an incoming request?
keyPoints: Route: the framework matches the request's URL to the correct handler function
Handle: the handler runs the business logic, reading and validating input from the request object
Data: it queries or updates the database (using parameterised queries) — the only tier that touches the Store
Respond: it builds and returns a response, e.g. HTML rendered via a template engine, or JSON
questions.explanation: The web server (nginx) handles the connection and static files and forwards dynamic requests to the framework (Flask).

questions.q: How do caching and a CDN reduce a web page's load time?
keyPoints: Caching stores frequently used data closer to where it's needed so it needn't be re-downloaded or re-computed (browser caching of assets, server caching of expensive query results)
A CDN is geographically distributed servers that cache static assets on an edge server near the user, cutting latency and offloading the origin
Both are the same 'store it closer to the user, reuse it' principle seen in DNS caching
Caveat: never publicly cache private/per-user or fast-changing content, or you serve stale or leaked data
